{{Short description|Theorem in mathematics}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''rearrangement inequality'''<ref>{{Citation | last1 = Hardy | first1 = G.H. | author-link =  G. H. Hardy | last2 = Littlewood | first2 = J.E. | author2-link = John Edensor Littlewood | last3 = Pólya | first3 = G. | author3-link = George Pólya | title = Inequalities | publisher = [[Cambridge University Press]] | series = Cambridge Mathematical Library | edition = 2. | year = 1952 | location = [[Cambridge]] | isbn = 0-521-05206-8 | mr = 0046395 | zbl = 0047.05302}}, Section&nbsp;10.2, Theorem&nbsp;368</ref> states that for every choice of [[real number]]s
<math display=block>x_1 \le \cdots \le x_n \quad \text{ and } \quad y_1 \le \cdots \le y_n</math>
and every [[permutation]] <math>\sigma</math> of the numbers <math>1, 2, \ldots n</math> we have
{{NumBlk|:|<math> x_1 y_n  + \cdots + x_n y_1
\le x_1 y_{\sigma(1)} + \cdots + x_n y_{\sigma(n)} 
\le x_1 y_1 + \cdots + x_n y_n</math>.|{{EquationRef|1}}}}
Informally, this means that in these types of sums, the largest sum is achieved by pairing large <math>x</math> values with large <math>y</math> values, and the smallest sum is achieved by pairing small values with large values. This can be formalised in the case that the <math>x_1, \ldots, x_n</math> are distinct, meaning that
<math>x_1 < \cdots < x_n,</math> then: 
#  The upper bound in ({{EquationNote|1}}) is attained only for permutations <math>\sigma</math> that keep the order of <math>y_1, \ldots, y_n,</math> that is, <math display=block>y_{\sigma(1)} \le \cdots \le y_{\sigma(n)},</math> or equivalently <math>(y_1,\ldots,y_n) = (y_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,y_{\sigma(n)}).</math> Such a <math>\sigma</math> can permute the indices of <math>y</math>-values that are equal; in the case <math>y_1 = \cdots = y_n</math> every permutation keeps the order of <math>y_1, \ldots, y_n.</math> If <math>y_1 < \cdots < y_n,</math> then the only such <math>\sigma</math> is the identity.
#  Correspondingly, the lower bound in ({{EquationNote|1}}) is attained only for permutations <math>\sigma</math> that reverse the order of <math>y_1, \ldots, y_n,</math> meaning that <math display=block>y_{\sigma(1)} \ge \cdots \ge y_{\sigma(n)}.</math> If <math>y_1 < \cdots < y_n,</math> then <math>\sigma(i) = n - i + 1</math> for all <math>i = 1, \ldots, n,</math> is the only permutation to do this.
Note that the rearrangement inequality ({{EquationNote|1}}) makes no assumptions on the signs of the real numbers, unlike inequalities such as the [[AM-GM Inequality|arithmetic-geometric mean inequality]].

{{TOC right}}

==Applications==

Many important inequalities can be proved by the rearrangement inequality, such as the [[Inequality of arithmetic and geometric means|arithmetic mean – geometric mean inequality]], the [[Cauchy–Schwarz inequality]], and [[Chebyshev's sum inequality]].

As a simple example, consider real numbers <math>x_1 \le \cdots \le x_n</math>: By applying ({{EquationNote|1}}) with <math>y_i := x_i</math> for all <math>i = 1,\ldots,n,</math> it follows that
<math display=block>x_1 x_n + \cdots + x_n x_1
\le x_1 x_{\sigma(1)} + \cdots + x_n x_{\sigma(n)}
\le x_1^2 + \cdots + x_n^2</math>
for every permutation <math>\sigma</math> of <math>1, \ldots, n.</math>

==Intuition==

The rearrangement inequality can be regarded as intuitive in the following way. Imagine there is a heap of $10 bills, a heap of $20 bills and one more heap of $100 bills. You are allowed to take 7 bills from a heap of your choice and then the heap disappears. In the second round you are allowed to take 5 bills from another heap and the heap disappears. In the last round you may take 3 bills from the last heap. In what order do you want to choose the heaps to maximize your profit? Obviously, the best you can do is to gain <math>7\cdot100 + 5\cdot20 + 3\cdot10</math> dollars. This is exactly what the upper bound of the rearrangement inequality ({{EquationNote|1}}) says for the sequences <math>3 < 5 < 7</math> and <math>10 < 20 < 100.</math> In this sense, it can be considered as an example of a [[greedy algorithm]].

==Geometric interpretation==

Assume that <math>0 < x_1 < \cdots < x_n</math> and <math> 0< y_1 < \cdots < y_n.</math> Consider a rectangle of width <math>x_1 + \cdots + x_n</math> and height <math>y_1 + \cdots + y_n,</math> subdivided into <math>n</math> columns of widths <math>x_1,\ldots,x_n</math> and the same number of rows of heights <math>y_1,\ldots,y_n,</math> so there are <math>\textstyle n^2</math> small rectangles. You are supposed to take <math>n</math> of these, one from each column and one from each row. The rearrangement inequality ({{EquationNote|1}}) says that you optimize the total area of your selection by taking the rectangles on the diagonal or the antidiagonal. 

==Proofs==

===Proof by contradiction===

The lower bound and the corresponding discussion of equality follow by applying the results for the upper bound to
<math display="inline">- y_n \le \cdots \le - y_1</math>, that is, let <math>\upsilon</math> be any permutation of the numbers <math display="inline">1, 2, \ldots n</math> we have <math display="inline">x_1 (-y_{\upsilon(1)})+\cdots +x_n (-y_{\upsilon (n)})\leq x_1 (-y_{n})+\cdots +x_n (-y_{1})</math>. Then, <math display="inline">x_1 y_{n}+\cdots +x_n y_{1}\leq x_1 y_{\upsilon(1)}+\cdots +x_n y_{\upsilon (n)}</math> for every permutation <math>\upsilon</math> of <math>1, \dots ,n</math>.

Therefore, it suffices to prove the upper bound in ({{EquationNote|1}}) and discuss when equality holds. 
Since there are only finitely many permutations of <math>1,\ldots,n,</math> there exists at least one <math>\sigma</math> for which the middle term in ({{EquationNote|1}})
<math display="block">x_1 y_{\sigma(1)} + \cdots + x_n y_{\sigma(n)}</math>
is maximal. In case there are several permutations with this property, let σ denote one with the highest number of integers <math>i</math> from <math>\{1,\ldots,n\}</math> satisfying <math>y_i = y_{\sigma(i)}.</math>

We will now [[reductio ad absurdum|prove by contradiction]], that <math>\sigma</math> has to keep the order of <math>y_1,\ldots,y_n</math> (then we are done with the upper bound in ({{EquationNote|1}}), because the identity has that property). Assume that there exists a <math>j\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}</math> such that <math>y_i = y_{\sigma(i)}</math> for all <math>i\in\{1,\ldots,j-1\}</math> and <math>y_j \neq y_{\sigma(j)}.</math> Hence <math>y_j < y_{\sigma(j)}</math> and there has to exist a <math>k\in\{j+1,\ldots,n\}</math> with <math>y_j = y_{\sigma(k)}</math> to fill the gap. Therefore,
{{NumBlk|:|<math> x_j \le x_k
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y_{\sigma(k)} < y_{\sigma(j)},</math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}
which implies that
{{NumBlk|:|<math> 0 \le (x_k - x_j)(y_{\sigma(j)} - y_{\sigma(k)}).</math>|{{EquationRef|3}}}}
Expanding this product and rearranging gives
{{NumBlk|:|<math> x_j y_{\sigma(j)} + x_k y_{\sigma(k)} \le x_j y_{\sigma(k)} + x_k y_{\sigma(j)}\,,</math>|{{EquationRef|4}}}}
which is equivalent to ({{EquationNote|3}}). Hence the permutation
<math display=block>\tau(i):=\begin{cases}\sigma(i)&\text{for }i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{j,k\},\\
\sigma(k)&\text{for }i = j,\\
\sigma(j)&\text{for }i = k,\end{cases}</math>
which arises from <math>\sigma</math> by exchanging the values <math>\sigma(j)</math> and <math>\sigma(k),</math> has at least one additional point which keeps the order compared to <math>\sigma,</math> namely at <math>j</math> satisfying <math>y_j=y_{\tau(j)},</math> and also attains the maximum in ({{EquationNote|1}}) due to ({{EquationNote|4}}). This contradicts the choice of <math>\sigma.</math>

If <math>x_1 < \cdots < x_n,</math> then we have strict inequalities in ({{EquationNote|2}}), ({{EquationNote|3}}), and ({{EquationNote|4}}), hence the maximum can only be attained by permutations keeping the order of <math>y_1 \le \cdots \le y_n,</math> and every other permutation <math>\sigma</math> cannot be optimal.

===Proof by induction===

As above, it suffices to treat the upper bound in ({{EquationNote|1}}). For a proof by [[mathematical induction]], we start with <math>n=2.</math> Observe that 
<math display=block>x_1 \le x_2 \quad \text{ and } \quad y_1 \le y_2</math>
implies that
{{NumBlk|:|<math>0 \le (x_2 - x_1) (y_2 - y_1),</math>|{{EquationRef|5}}}}
which is equivalent to
{{NumBlk|:|<math>x_1 y_2 + x_2 y_1 \le  x_1 y_1 + x_2 y_2,</math>|{{EquationRef|6}}}}
hence the upper bound in ({{EquationNote|1}}) is true for <math>n = 2.</math>
If <math>x_1 < x_2,</math> then we get strict inequality in ({{EquationNote|5}}) and ({{EquationNote|6}}) if and only if <math>y_1 < y_2.</math> Hence only the identity, which is the only permutation here keeping the order of <math>y_1 < y_2,</math> gives the maximum.

As an induction hypothesis assume that the upper bound in the rearrangement inequality ({{EquationNote|1}}) is true for <math>n-1</math> with <math>n\ge3</math> and that in the case <math>x_1 <\cdots <x_{n-1}</math> there is equality only when the permutation <math>\sigma</math> of <math>1,\ldots,n-1</math> keeps the order of <math>y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1}.</math>

Consider now <math>x_1 \le \cdots \le x_n</math> and <math>y_1 \le \cdots \le y_n.</math> Take a <math>\sigma</math> from the finite number of permutations of <math>1,\ldots,n</math> such that the rearrangement in the middle of ({{EquationNote|1}}) gives the maximal result. There are two cases:

* If <math>\sigma(n)=n,</math> then <math>y_n=y_{\sigma(n)}</math> and, using the induction hypothesis, the upper bound in ({{EquationNote|1}}) is true with equality and <math>\sigma</math> keeps the order of <math>y_1,\ldots,y_{n-1},y_n</math> in the case <math>x_1 < \cdots < x_n.</math>
* If <math>k := \sigma(n) < n,</math> then there is a <math>j\in\{1,\dots,n-1\}</math> with <math>\sigma(j)=n.</math> Define the permutation <math display=block>\tau(i)=\begin{cases}\sigma(i)&\text{for }i \in \{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\{j,n\},\\
k&\text{for }i = j,\\
n&\text{for }i = n,\end{cases}</math> which arises from <math>\sigma</math> by exchanging the values of <math>j</math> and <math>n.</math> There are now two subcases:
# If <math>x_j = x_{\sigma_j} = x_n</math> or <math>y_n = y_{\sigma_n} = y_k,</math> then this exchange of values of <math>\sigma</math> has no effect on the middle term in ({{EquationNote|1}}) because <math>\tau</math> gives the same sum, and we can proceed by applying the first case to <math>\tau.</math> Note that in the case <math>x_1 < \cdots < x_n,</math> the permutation <math>\tau</math> keeps the order of <math>y_1,\ldots,y_n</math> if and only if <math>\sigma</math> does.
# If <math>x_j < x_n</math> and <math>y_k < y_n,</math> then <math>0 < (x_n - x_j) (y_n - y_k),</math> which is equivalent to <math>x_j y_{\sigma_j}+ x_n y_{\sigma_n} < x_j y_{\tau_j} + x_n y_{{\tau_n}}</math> and shows that <math>\sigma</math> is not optimal, hence this case cannot happen due to the choice of <math>\sigma.</math>

==Generalizations==

===Three or more sequences===
A straightforward generalization takes into account more sequences. Assume we have finite ordered sequences of nonnegative real numbers
<math display=block>0 \le x_1\le\cdots\le x_n\quad\text{and}\quad 0\le y_1\le\cdots\le y_n\quad\text{and}\quad 0\le z_1\le\cdots\le z_n</math>
and a permutation <math>y_{\sigma(1)},\ldots,y_{\sigma(n)}</math> of <math>y_1,\dots,y_n</math> and another permutation <math>z_{\tau(1)},\dots,z_{\tau(n)}</math> of <math>z_1,\dots,z_n.</math> Then
<math display=block> x_1 y_{\sigma(1)} z_{\tau(1)} + \cdots + x_n y_{\sigma(n)} z_{\tau(n)} \le x_1 y_1 z_1 + \cdots + x_n y_n z_n.</math>

Unlike the standard rearrangement inequality ({{EquationNote|1}}), this statement requires the numbers to be nonnegative. A similar statement is true for any number of sequences with all numbers nonnegative.

===Functions instead of factors===
Another generalization of the rearrangement inequality states that for all [[real number]]s <math>x_1 \le \cdots \le x_n</math> and every choice of continuously [[differentiable function]]s <math>f_i: [x_1,x_n] \to \R</math> for <math>i = 1, 2, \ldots, n</math> such that their derivatives <math>f'_1,\ldots,f'_n</math> satisfy
<math display=block>f'_1(x) \le f'_2(x) \le \cdots \le f'_n(x) \quad \text{ for all } x \in [x_1,x_n],</math>
the inequality
<math display=block>\sum_{i=1}^n f_{n-i+1}(x_i) \le \sum_{i=1}^n f_{\sigma(i)}(x_i) \le \sum_{i=1}^n f_i(x_i)</math>
holds for every [[permutation]] <math>f_{\sigma(1)}, \ldots, f_{\sigma(n)}</math> of <math>f_1, \ldots, f_n.</math><ref>{{citation | year=2017 | last=Holstermann | first=Jan | title=A Generalization of the Rearrangement Inequality | periodical=Mathematical Reflections | issue = 5 (2017) | url=https://www.awesomemath.org/wp-pdf-files/math-reflections/mr-2017-05/rearrangement_inequality.pdf}}</ref>
Taking real numbers <math>y_1 \le \cdots \le y_n</math> and the linear functions <math>f_i(x) := x y_i</math> for real <math>x</math> and <math>i = 1,\ldots,n,</math> the standard rearrangement inequality ({{EquationNote|1}}) is recovered.
